items.title: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
items.summary: The report says there are signs of possible contamination across almost all of Gaza as a result of Israel's actions.
items.body:
Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images

Image caption,

The UN estimates that Israeli forces dropped more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives on Gaza in almost two years (file photo)

ByYolande Knell

Middle East correspondent, Reporting fromJerusalem

Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the non-profit organisation Oxfam says, external.

Heavy metals, explosive residues, and asbestos from destroyed buildings, dioxins and biological contaminants in the air, soil and water supply are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.

Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, accuses Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza."

"The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival," he says.

Israel's government has been asked for its response to the report.

It has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. Israel maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.

Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images

Image caption,

The report says 99% of Gaza shows indicators of potential environmental contamination

Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.

The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".

Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.

"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.

She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.

Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Only a small fraction of the more than 60 million tonnes of debris in Gaza has been cleared

With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.

Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.

UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.

The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Recent winter storms caused rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent camps

Already, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.

A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps.

"There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."

Image caption,

Dr Alaa Abu Hajar has seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war

Farmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe.

"Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.

Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

The high street retailer said its own systems had not been compromised by the hack. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

The high street retailer said its own systems had not been compromised by the hack. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

Next issues cyber-attack warning after ‘benign’ data accessed by hackers

Retailer says it believes no personal data that could lead to fraud was accessed after hack of third-party supplier

• Business live – latest updates

Next has warned that hackers have gained access to data relating to the clothing and homewares retailer through a technology supplier.

The firm said on Monday that it had been informed that one of its third-party suppliers had “experienced a cyber incident” resulting in unauthorised access to the data.

The high street chain said it believed that customers’ personal data had not been compromised and the information affected was “limited in nature and, based on our current assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against our customers or Next”.

It is understood the data accessed does not include information such as contact details, addresses, passwords or bank details, which could be used to commit fraud.

It said Next’s systems had not been compromised, though it was “affecting the supplier’s environment” in its business.

Investigations into the hack are in progress. Next said in a statement to investors: “Despite the limited and benign nature of the affected data, we are treating the matter with the utmost seriousness and are working closely with the supplier, law enforcement and relevant regulatory authorities.”

The latest incident comes amid a spate of cyber-attacks against high-profile retailers around the world.

Last week it emerged that a secret UK government cybersecurity operation had warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums.

That came after hackers caused many millions of euros of damage in continental Europe, with attacks on fridge and freezer control systems in recent months.

Fashion retailers including the owner of Hobbs and Whistles, TFG London, and the online fashion seller Asos have faced cyber-attacks in which customer data was accessed.

Last year, several other British retailers, including Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Harrods, were hit by damaging cyber incidents which affected operations for months.

items.title: Haigh tells CBI that even US which is ‘hardly a hotbed of socialism’ has more public control of utilities than UK – UK politics live
items.summary: First secretary of state gives further detail on Burnham’s plans and says the government is not against the markets In her speech, Louise Haigh announced that Juergen Maier, chair of Great British Energy, has been appointed as the government’s northern economy and reindustrialisation commissioner. S…
items.body:
In her speech to the CBI, Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, delivered one of the most detailed explanations we have had from a minister as to what Andy Burnham means when he calls for more public control of utilities.

She said that the government was not against markets, and that in areas like telecoms privatisation had worked. But in water and energy it hadn’t, she insisted. She suggested that, in wanting more public control in these sectors, the government was aligned with the US, “hardly a hotbed of state socialism”.

She said:

Now I know the word privatisation can start an argument. So let me be precise. This is not about whether markets work. They do. Where there is genuine competition, as in telecoms, markets have given consumers choice and kept prices low while delivering infrastructure.
The social licence to operate must be won every day by building trust and having the best value, product or service. Where competition exists, it should be left to thrive, supported by our strong, independent Competition and Markets Authority.
But when it comes to essential services, we have spent four decades trying and failing to recreate market conditions when consumers have no alternative.
Public control is about getting the right outcomes. It’s not ideological. Ownership is not a requirement. We took the railway back into public ownership because it wasn’t working for passengers or the taxpayer. But we want Great British Railways to be challenged by open access operators in Greater Manchester’s Bee Network, which you may have heard of. Routes are set by the elected mayor to benefit the community. The services are still run by private operators.
Delivering the homes we need depends on a buoyant developer sector.
Looking at water and energy, we must accept that the status quo is not the neutral, pragmatic, centre ground. It’s the outlier, an exception that no other nation is trying to emulate.
Around the world, the core infrastructure of water overwhelmingly stays in public hands. England is almost unique in handing the entire system to private owners. The only other country in that corner with us is Chile.
We are also one of the few countries in Europe whose electricity and gas transmission networks are entirely privately owned. And here’s the irony. Foreign governments now own a bigger share of our utilities than the British government does – significant stakes in our water, electricity and gas networks, returns paid to their taxpayers.
I welcome that investment. Let me be clear about that. But it raises a question: why do other governments see the strategic and commercial value in holding Britain’s essential assets, when for 40 years the British government couldn’t?
And it isn’t just Europe. Look at the United States of America, hardly a hotbed of state socialism. Most Americans get their water from a public utility. Fewer than one in 10 get it from a private one. Community-owned power companies serve one in seven American electricity customers in Los Angeles and Seattle, in Nashville, in Austin, and the federal government still owns the Tennessee Valley Authority, one of the biggest power companies in the country. Nobody thinks America is anti-business.
So let’s be honest with ourselves. The status quo is the ideological position, and saying so should not be taboo.

Haigh also said that past governments had resorted to trying to make the privatisation of utilities work through excessive regulation.

To make the experiment work, successive governments leant on regulation, first to try to recreate competition from monopolies through a spreadsheet; then to manage what private markets would never price on their own, like the spare capacity that keeps the lights on; then to deliver social policy, treated as a free good because it went on the bill, not the budget.
Ofgem now has six times the staff it had in the early 2000s, almost three times the administrative budget in real terms, and a rule book more than six times longer. We’ve got a hulking, complex behemoth of a regulatory state. It satisfies no one. Not consumers, not investors. When you prioritise everything, you prioritise nothing.
In the fog of complexity, bad actors can thrive, while the rest of us can’t move with a clarity and pace this moment demands.
That is why public control should not alarm anyone in this room. It’s not ideological. It’s pragmatic, and it’s essential – for people, for places, and for business.
We will measure our progress against three tests: affordability, investability, accountability.

Louise Haigh at the CBI. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA

items.body:
Onboard view of maritime drone approaching vessel off Benghazi on Sunday. Photograph: Volodymyr Zelenskyy/Telegram/Reuters

Onboard view of maritime drone approaching vessel off Benghazi on Sunday. Photograph: Volodymyr Zelenskyy/Telegram/Reuters

Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya

Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship

• Europe live – latest updates

Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.

Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.

“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.

Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.

locator map

In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”

Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.

The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hitthe Kerch bridge - a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic sea port of Kaliningrad.

Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.

Large blaze at Benghazi port after suspected drone attack on Russian warship – video

Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.

At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.

Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.

Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.

More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, the Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.

The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli said in a statement it was alarmed by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.

There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”

Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.

In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.

Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.

In April, the Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli said in a statement it was alarmed by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.

There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”

Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.

In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.

Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.

The Freelander 8, the first Freelander-branded electric vehicle jointly developed by British carmaker Jaguar Land Rover and Chinese joint-venture partner Chery displayed at a launch event in Wuhu, China. Photograph: Nick Carey/Reuters

The Freelander 8, the first Freelander-branded electric vehicle jointly developed by British carmaker Jaguar Land Rover and Chinese joint-venture partner Chery displayed at a launch event in Wuhu, China. Photograph: Nick Carey/Reuters

Flagship UK gigafactory plan in turmoil after it loses second builder in five months

Tata-owned Agratas plant to build EV batteries for sister company Jaguar Land Rover seen as crucial for long-term health of British car industry

One of the UK’s flagship electric vehicle battery projects has been thrown into turmoil after its second building contractor in five months walked away, adding to questions over when Jaguar Land Rover cars will use British-made batteries.

The £5.2bn gigafactory in Bridgwater, Somerset, is being built by Agratas, to provide batteries for Britain’s largest automotive employer, its sister company. Agratas and Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) are both part of Indian conglomerate Tata Group.

The UK government has pledged £380m in financial support for the factory because it is seen as crucial to the long-term survival of the British car industry, but the build has suffered several setbacks. The construction specialist contracted by Agratas, TSL, has decided to leave the project after failing to agree terms with Agratas, according to three sources.

Batteries are among the important parts of EVs, but global supply is now dominated by China, South Korea and Japan. Successive Conservative and Labour governments have strongly supported efforts to build a British battery supply chain, and it also fits with Andy Burnham’s hopes to “reindustrialise” the UK. Not all of the subsidy has yet been paid out.

Tata announced the gigafactory in 2023, aiming for a 2026 start of production with as many as 4,200 employees, before pushing it back to 2027. Replacing the lead contractor for the second time in five months is likely to add to doubts over whether Agratas can hit its latest target of January 2028 – although the company has not yet pushed back its planned start date.

A spokesperson for Agratas said: “We are on track to meet our customer requirements.

“The Somerset site is a large and complex industrialisation project, and all of our supplier partners are supporting us well as we prepare for the facility’s launch phase.”

The inability to reach an agreement with TSL, formally known as Tonroe Group, stemmed from disagreements over the timeline and cost of the project, two sources said.

TSL is expected to leave the site within two or three months, leaving no other main build contractor lined up. However, it is thought that NG Bailey, the project’s mechanical, electrical and plumbing contractor, could be one option to take over the entire build.

The issues at the heart of the dispute are similar to those with TSL’s predecessor, Sir Robert McAlpine (SRM). Agratas fired SRM at short notice in June, and one source suggested discussions over the terms of its departure remain ongoing.

Morale within Agratas has also been hit by the company’s decision to relocate some workers from Coventry, in a building shared with other Tata Group companies, to Somerset.

Some of those workers are expected to take redundancy rather than uproot families and move 120 miles away. If they did so it would continue a stream of senior staff leaving the business in recent months, two sources said.

The UK’s only operating gigafactory, AESC’s plant in Sunderland, north-east England, has also faced problems as carmakers have scaled back plans for EVs, with governments delaying bans on petrol and diesel cars. The Guardian revealed in August that AESC had shelved expansion plans after it failed to agree a separate deal to supply JLR.

after newsletter promotion

It is understood that JLR has secured batteries from other suppliers, so its plans to increase sales of new electric Land Rovers and Jaguars will not be affected. However, those initial cars will not have British-made batteries, although the manufacturer could also avoid EU tariffs under “rules of origin” if it uses batteries made in Europe.

Agratas has made some progress at the Somerset factory, as well as another site in Sanand, western India. Some Agratas managers have travelled to India this week to share experiences with their counterparts in India and discuss the UK situation.

The shell of the building site in south west England is mostly complete, and National Grid has started work on the electricity substation that will provide the large amounts of power needed to make batteries.

People close to the project suggest Agratas could still succeed in producing batteries and avoid the fate of an earlier rival project, Britishvolt, which collapsed after failing to secure firm orders. The former Britishvolt site in north-east England is now being turned into a datacentre for artificial intelligence – a potentially attractive prospect for an empty building with a high-capacity connection to the electricity grid.

Agratas was approached for comment. TSL declined to comment. JLR declined to comment. NG Bailey was approached for comment.

items.body: More than two weeks of talks in Turkey fail to produce a resolution to tackle climate crisis. Plus, a savage review of Melania’s new documentary Good morning. The world’s nations have failed to reach agreement at the Cop31 talks in Turkey. In a dramatic conclusion to the summit, major powers rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels. The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien. What was in the proposed agreement? The Antalya pact invited nations to electrify their economies, called on wealthy countries to fund climate adaptation for poorer ones, and urged signatories to minimise any “overshoot” of the Paris agreement’s 1.5C global heating threshold. However, it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” demanded by more than 130 countries, instead including controversial provisions on carbon capture and storage technology that critics argued would perpetuate fossil fuel use. What precipitated the collapse of the talks? In this analysis piece , the Guardian’s environment editor, who was at Cop, explains that after a marathon negotiating session ran more than 40 hours past its deadline, a small group led by Saudi Arabia refused to accept any mention of a “transition away from fossil fuels”. While such holdouts would normally force through a watered-down compromise, nearly 40 nations – led by the EU, the UK, small islands and least developed countries – broke with precedent and openly rejected the weakened text, refusing to salvage the usual face-saving semblance of unity. items.title: Flights grounded in Belgium due to strike against austerity measures
items.summary: A series of strikes have hit Belgium in recent months as the prime minister struggles to agree a budget to cut costs.
items.body:
Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Brussels Airport is receiving no travellers until 21:00 on Monday

ByPaulin Kola

Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and train services have been severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.

All air traffic has been halted in Zaventem airport in the capital, Brussels, as well as Charlerois, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.

Trains and underground services have also been halted in Brussels where large numbers of people are expected to join a protest march.

The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever has so far failed to agree a budget to cut costs with his coalition allies. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.

No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers. More than 50,000 travellers' plans were being disrupted - with more expected to be affected overnight and on Tuesday.

A similar situation has affected Charlerois, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure of arrival.

"Without air traffic control, no flights can take off or land," the airport said on Saturday when the strike action was announced, warning of "disastrous consequences".

As thousands descended on Brussels for the protest march, the leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".

"A genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes," Bert Engelaar, head of FGBT, said.

"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," Engelaar said, praising the left-wing Vooruit party - the only member of the five-party governing coalition reported to have stalled efforts to agree the budget.

Vooruit wants to raise taxes on the rich, and fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.

Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.

Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.

items.title: Presidential villa also hit by water and power cuts, Nigerian leader says
items.summary: Bola Tinubu says he was shaving last week when the water cut out - an experience familiar to many Nigerians.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Tinubu made the disclosure at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family

ByMansur Abubakar

Reporting fromAbuja

Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water - failures that plague ordinary citizens.

He said he was shaving last week when the water supply at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja cut.

He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to address these issues..

Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family in Lagos.

He explained: "On the Wednesday of last week, I was shaving, and the water went off. In the villa, you won't know punishment dey dia too [there’s punishment there too in Nigerian pidgin].

"The water went off. So we will correct all this. No light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have just started. We can do it, and we will do it for Nigeria,” he said.

Aso Villa serves as both the office and official residence of the Nigerian president. It is situated at the base of Aso Rock in Abuja.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Many Nigerians rely on generators like these to power their homes and businesses

Nigeria has long endured electricity shortages, but recent severe disruptions have been caused primarily by insufficient gas supplies and declining hydropower output, rather than the usual nationwide grid collapse.

Persistent blackouts in Lagos, Abuja and elsewhere have forced distribution companies to implement rotating power cuts, severely impacting households and businesses.

The country also suffers from chronic water shortages, the result of a structural crisis rooted in the gap between rapid urban population growth and decaying, inadequate public water infrastructure.

Tinubu made a high-profile electricity promise during the 2023 election campaign, but the exact wording and how binding it is has become a major point of contention ahead of the 16 January election.

Tinubu defeated the country’s former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as well as Peter Obi in 2023 and the three are seen as the strongest contenders once again.

items.title: Trump administration deported US citizen to Mexico, DoJ admits in court
items.summary: Brian Morales García of Texas seeks damages after he was wrongly identified as undocumented in case White House wants dropped The Trump administration recently admitted in federal court that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after American authorities incorrectly concluded he was an undocumented im…
items.body:
Court filings recount how border patrol agent Robert Gil Jr consulted records from Mexico that listed a Mexican birthplace for Brian Morales. Photograph: Dominic Gwinn/Middle East Images/AFP/Getty Images

Court filings recount how border patrol agent Robert Gil Jr consulted records from Mexico that listed a Mexican birthplace for Brian Morales. Photograph: Dominic Gwinn/Middle East Images/AFP/Getty Images

Trump administration deported US citizen to Mexico, DoJ admits in court

Brian Morales García of Texas seeks damages after he was wrongly identified as undocumented in case White House wants dropped

The Trump administration recently admitted in federal court that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after American authorities incorrectly concluded he was an undocumented immigrant.

Attorneys for the US justice department made that admission on Friday while requesting the dismissal of a lawsuit for damages that the deported man – Brian José Morales García of Austin, Texas – has been pursuing against the federal government.

Morales García’s case took that turn as the White House has faced bipartisan criticism for the aggressive mass deportation campaign pursued by Donald Trump throughout his second presidency – widely seen as a factor in the electoral battering his Republican party suffered during the 3 November midterms, costing it control of Congress.

The Denver-born, Mexico-raised Morales García was riding with his boss to his job as an air-conditioning installation technician on 3 April when they were pulled over by state and local officers near Fredericksburg, Texas.

They went out to celebrate at a Memphis bar. Then, ICE descended

Read more

Morales García was his boss’s passenger and did not have his identification on him. The 25-year-old also told the officers that he had his birth certificate and social security card at home, but they didn’t believe him – so they called immigration agents, who detained Morales García.

Court filings recount how Robert Gil Jr, a US Customs and Border Protection agent, consulted records from Mexico that listed a Mexican birthplace for Morales García. Gil Jr also accused Morales García of saying he was born in Mexico and observed that he only spoke in Spanish, according to court records.

Morales García was deported on 7 April, with the Trump administration later accusing him in a media statement of being in the country illegally.

Morales García’s attorneys sued on 1 May, maintaining that he had falsely said he entered the US illegally and signed papers for a rapid deportation in response to threats of imprisonment by agents. His lawsuit, which seeks an unspecified amount of money, also contended that family and friends tried to deliver documents proving his US citizenship before this deportation.

But those efforts were unduly rebuffed, Morales García’s lawsuit said.

The Trump administration denied Morales García’s assertions, saying on Friday that he went to Mexico voluntarily and therefore lacked any basis to sue the federal government for damages. Nonetheless, in court filings on Friday, the administration conceded that Morales García “was permitted entry” back into the US on 30 August after it reviewed “information concerning plaintiff’s place of birth”.

“Plaintiff is a dual citizen of the United States and Mexico,” Justin Simmons, the US attorney for the western district of Texas, wrote in a court filing first reported by the Texas Tribune.

Judge says ICE ‘made a mockery of court orders’ with instant re-arrest policy

Read more

Americans are not required to carry proof of citizenship when going about their daily business. Lawyers across the US have seen cases such as Morales García’s, which begin after an encounter with local authorities demonstrate how those officials are generally not aware of the nuances of immigration policy.

Texas’s public safety department is among many US state and local agencies that collaborate with federal immigration authorities under their 287(g) program.

The judge presiding over Morales García’s lawsuit, Robert Lee Pitman, did not immediately rule on the Trump administration’s request on Friday to dismiss the case. The lawsuit also named unspecified local and state Texas law enforcement officers as defendants.

An October 2025 report by ProPublica found that immigration agents had detained more than 170 US citizens during the first nine months of Trump’s second presidency.

Meanwhile, the media statement incorrectly saying Morales García was in the US illegally is among several related to immigration enforcement under the Trump administration that has unraveled under scrutiny.

A Guardian analysis published in July reviewed Trump administration press releases on 26 cases of cars allegedly being used to assault immigration enforcement agents – and nearly all were either disproven or dropped.

items.body:
It is proposed that visitor numbers will be limited to between 600 and 1,000 a day in June to September. Photograph: Nicolas Escobar/Getty Images

It is proposed that visitor numbers will be limited to between 600 and 1,000 a day in June to September. Photograph: Nicolas Escobar/Getty Images

Chamonix mayor plans tourist limits for Alpine beauty spot

Rising numbers around Lac Blanc are having big impact on environment and on visitors’ enjoyment, mayor says

In the Alpine town of Chamonix, most tourist paths lead to the national park with spectacular views across Mont Blanc and the shrinking blue glaciers. In the summer, up to 4,000 tourists a day hike or take the cable car to the lakes high in the Aiguilles Rouges nature reserve.

Many of them descend disappointed. Once a place of nature and tranquility, the beauty spot’s visitor numbers have more than doubled since 2020, spoiling the experience and leaving trails of litter, threatening the environment and wildlife.

Now Chamonix plans to become the first town in the Alps to introduce visitor quotas, to limit the number of hikers around Lac Blanc and the Lacs des Chéserys.

The town’s mayor, Francois-Xavier Laffin, announced last week that from next June tourists would be required to book in advance to visit the area. After booking, they will receive a QR code granting them access.

People visit the ice cave of the Mer de Glace glacier in Chamonix. Photograph: Delpixart/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Laffin championed the quotas after visiting Marseille, where a similar scheme was introduced limiting access to the Calanques national park in 2022. He said the aim was “reserve to preserve”, adding that visiting the mountains would still be free but subject to conditions.

Laffin said mass tourism was having a major impact on the environment, wildlife and on visitors’ enjoyment of the reserve. “Lac Blanc is one place we cannot let continue to deteriorate” he said, adding that the council was looking at additional regulations in other areas.

The plan, which needs the final approval of the local prefect, would restrict the number of visitors to the Lac Blanc area to between 600 and 1,000 a day for four months from June to September.

Christian Schwoehrer, the director of the Haute-Savoie Nature Conservation Agency, which manages the reserve, said: “We will see how it works for the next three years and if it does then it will be extended and maybe applied to other areas. This is a nature reserve but when there are thousands of visitors a day there’s no peace for the protected species or local people and we need stronger measures to control this.

“At points of entry [to the reserve] there will be ‘eco guards’ to verify that people have reserved. If they haven’t, they could be fined, though our intention is to avoid fining people by making sure they know in advance and cannot say they weren’t warned.”

Visitors near Lac Blanc in the Aiguilles Rouge nature reserve above Chamonix. Photograph: Simon Turner/Alamy

The quota plan has met some local opposition from the land’s legal owners. Lac Blanc sits in just under 3 square miles of private estate held by 35 families under a historic entity that has existed for centuries and is now managed by the Montagne de Chéserys company.

One of the landowners, Guillaume Ravanel, a mountain guide, agreed tourist numbers need controlling but suggested visitors should be asked to pay a small entry fee to access the reserve.

Frédéric Charlet-Berguerand, a co-manager of Montagne de Chéserys, told Le Monde: “This quota system is innovative and virtuous.” Contacted by the Guardian, he added: “That said, there will be no quotas on our private property until they are approved by a meeting of the owners,” due to be held in December. “Let’s not put the cart before the horse.”

The mayor is also looking at tighter controls on the Ultra-Trail du Mont Blanc. Photograph: AscentXmedia/Getty Images

Laffin said the quota plan would cost about €590,000 for the three-year “experimental” period. Financing has yet to be arranged but he said part would be raised by Chamonix and other local authorities and the town would be applying for a grant from the government’s “green fund” to help protect the environment. Private sponsors are also being sought.

The mayor, elected in March, has made managing tourist numbers a priority. He is also looking at tighter controls on the three-week Ultra-Trail du Mont Blanc, an ultramarathon circling the Mont-Blanc massif through France, Italy and Switzerland that begins in Chamonix. The event, started in 2003, now attracts 10,000 runners and up to 50,000 visitors each August.

Schwoehrer said summer crowds meant local people were avoiding the reserve. A recent survey found that 55% of visitors who ascended to Lac Blanc said they were disappointed by the experience, he said.

“We don’t want to stop people going there, just have a few stronger rules. It’s a compromise to ensure that visitors have a good experience and at the same time the natural environment is protected.”

items.body:
Compass may move its primary listing to the US as soon as Tuesday. Photograph: Dado Ruvić/Reuters

Compass may move its primary listing to the US as soon as Tuesday. Photograph: Dado Ruvić/Reuters

NHS caterer Compass ‘plans stock market switch’ in blow to London

Surrey-based firm’s decision to move primary listing to New York would mark latest loss for FTSE 100

• Business live – latest updates

Compass, one of the biggest companies in the FTSE 100, is reportedly planning to switch its primary listing from London to the US in the latest hit to the struggling UK stock market.

The £43.6bn ($57bn) catering giant, which has been listed in London since 1988, could announce its intention to move its listing to New York as soon as Tuesday when it reports its annual results, according to the Financial Times.

The caterer is a major government contractor, providing meals in more than 2,000 schools, academies, colleges and universities across the UK and in some NHS hospitals, as well as offices in the private sector.

It also provides grab-and-go foods for fast food chains and cafes such as Starbucks, Costa and Taco Bell. Last year, the company made about three-quarters of its $3bn profit in North America.

Compass, which switched its reporting currency from British sterling to US dollars in October 2023, also changed the trading currency of its London-listed shares to US dollars in April this year.

The company, which is headquartered in Surrey and has more than 600,000 staff around the world, plans to retain a secondary listing in London and will say that there is no threat to its staff in the UK, according to the Telegraph.

Its potential departure would be the latest in a string of exits by companies seeking deeper pools of capital and higher valuations in the US.

In recent years, the equipment rental company Ashtead, the building material supplier CRH, and the owner of Paddy Power, Flutter Entertainment, have all moved their primary listings to the US.

The UK’s biggest drugmaker, AstraZeneca, listed its shares directly on the New York Stock Exchange this year, putting its US shares on an even footing with its London-listed stock.

A string of companies have also left London’s stock market after agreeing to takeover deals. The flurry of deal-making this year includes warehouse landlord Segro’s £14bn takeover by its US rival Prologis, easyJet’s £5.7bn takeover by the US private equity company Apollo and the £9.9bn takeover of asset manager Schroders by a US investor.

Other deals include the £10bn takeover of the lab testing group Intertek by a consortium led by the Swedish private equity company EQT in June. Beazley, the specialist insurer with clients including Lloyds of London, agreed an £8bn deal to be acquired by its larger rival Zurich in February.

Meanwhile, fewer companies are joining London’s stock market too, as the UK faces a dearth of flotations. There were just seven listings in the first half of this year, raising £577m in total, according to data from the professional services company EY.

Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, has been one of the few companies to join London’s market this year. The payments processor listed at £1.96 a share in October and traded at about £2.05 on Monday.

Compass was approached for comment.

items.body: Party that won just 0.2% of the vote in 2016 is on course for almost 20% this time and could be part of next government Almost exactly eight years ago, a video clip of a stocky, bearded man riding a horse through western Andalucía went viral in Spain . The rider was Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, the soundtrack was a bombastic snatch of the Lord of the Rings score, and the caption was an equally unsubtle callback to the 700-year fight to wrest the Iberian peninsula from Islamic rule. “La Reconquista comenzará en tierras andaluzas,” it read – the reconquest will begin on Andalucían soil. Celebrated by some, jeered by others – and inventively lampooned by those with sufficient skill and time on their hands – the video didn’t seem quite as amusing three weeks later when Vox broke through into the political mainstream by winning 12 seats in Andalucía’s regional parliament. A badger sett in Hambledon, Surrey. Haigh did not push back against the idea Natural England was being targeted for abolition. Photograph: Lillian King/Getty Images

Natural England could be abolished as part of quango cull, says Louise Haigh

First secretary of state says proliferation of arms-length government bodies is hampering decision-making

The nature watchdog Natural England could be abolished as part of a cull of arm’s length government organisations, Louise Haigh has said.

Saying that the proliferation of quangos and other similar bodies had made decision-making by ministers more difficult, the first secretary of state said it could fall within a push to change the landscape of government by scrapping some organisations and bringing others into departments.

Abolishing Natural England could be justified on the basis that it could speed up planning decisions and thus boost housebuilding and growth, but removing or curbing its role would be likely to prompt concern from environmental groups.

Last month, the Conservatives announced that if they won power they would abolish both Natural England and the Environment Agency, saying this would help create more new homes.

Louise Haigh: ‘We’re absolutely committed to devolving responsibilities where they can be devolved.’ Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA

Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, was speaking before a speech to the CBI conference on Monday morning at which she was to make the case for greater government control of public utilities.

After the Times reported Natural England was in line to be abolished, Haigh was asked on Sky News about the proliferation of quangos. She said: “We’ve had successive governments complain about this, but unfortunately, successive governments have created more of these and pushed more decision-making out of their own departments, so that then when they make decisions they don’t agree with, they turn around and look in horror.

“That’s why we’re absolutely committed to devolving responsibilities where they can be devolved.”

Asked if she was considering getting rid of Natural England, she said: “We’re considering all arm’slength bodies, both devolving, dissolving, and bringing back into departments, because we cannot continue with this situation where politicians look round and can’t take responsibility for the actions that people have elected their government for.”

Asked again about the specific fate of Natural England in a later interview on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Haigh again did not push back against the idea it was being targeted for abolition along with other arms-length bodies.

after newsletter promotion

She said: “So all the ALBs are in my sight for either devolving responsibilities that can be pushed down to mayors and strategic authorities, whether they can be brought back into departments under the direct power of the secretary of state, or whether they can be dissolved entirely.”

In a section of her speech about utilities, according to extracts released in advance, Haigh was to say she would “put pragmatism and public interest ahead of failed political ideology”, adding: “Public control is not anti-business – it’s about getting the foundations right, so that private enterprise can do what it does best.”

Saying almost no other nation had so many essential services run by private companies, and often overseas ones at that, Haigh was to say: “The status quo is not the neutral, pragmatic centre ground. It’s the outlier. An exception that no other nation is trying to emulate.”

blocks.text: Louise Haigh: ‘We’re absolutely committed to devolving responsibilities where they can be devolved.’ Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA
Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, was speaking before a speech to the CBI conference on Monday morning at which she was to make the case for greater government control of public utilities.

“That’s why we’re absolutely committed to devolving responsibilities where they can be devolved.”

Asked if she was considering getting rid of Natural England, she said: “We’re considering all arm’slength bodies, both devolving, dissolving, and bringing back into departments, because we cannot continue with this situation where politicians look round and can’t take responsibility for the actions that people have elected their government for.”

Asked again about the specific fate of Natural England in a later interview on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Haigh again did not push back against the idea it was being targeted for abolition along with other arms-length bodies.

She said: “So all the ALBs are in my sight for either devolving responsibilities that can be pushed down to mayors and strategic authorities, whether they can be brought back into departments under the direct power of the secretary of state, or whether they can be dissolved entirely.”

items.title: Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore ties after tensions over conflict
items.summary: The two leaders committed to upholding sovereignty and "non-interference in the internal affairs of states".
items.body:
Image source, William Ruto/X

Image caption,

The meeting between Kenya's President William Ruto (left) and DR Congo's Félix Tshisekedi (centre) was hosted by Denis Sassou Nguesso (right)

ByBasillioh Rukanga

Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.

This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.

On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".

The agreement was announced in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé as mediator.

Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".

DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).

DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.

DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.

When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was launched in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.

The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.

DR Congo said naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.

• Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader Published31 October

Relations deteriorated further after Kenya hosted a meeting of Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila, in October 2025.

Kabila was in 2025 sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself.

He has since been named the leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), the new rebel coalition that took over from the AFC.

Sunday's meeting between Ruto and Tshisekedi also included other issues including deepening trade cooperation, economic development, and regional integration.

The two also sought to collaborate to control the spread of the Ebola virus.

On Sunday, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said the frequency of attacks across the country's east had increased since the end of October, seriously affecting the Ebola response.

Tedros said heavy fighting in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged had disrupted work and the wider Ebola response.

More than 5,700 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.

The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.

items.title: Gas prices in Europe surge as forecast cold snap feeds supply shortage fears
items.summary: Jump in price follows slowdown in Qatar supplies and depleted summer stocks due to heatwaves Business live – latest updates European gas prices surged on Monday as a forecast cold snap in the coming weeks fed fears across the continent’s over depleted supply this winter and costly household bills. T…
items.body:
A cold snap is forecast across north-west Europe. Photograph: John Potter/Alamy

A cold snap is forecast across north-west Europe. Photograph: John Potter/Alamy

Gas prices in Europe surge as forecast cold snap feeds supply shortage fears

Jump in price follows slowdown in Qatar supplies and depleted summer stocks due to heatwaves

• Business live – latest updates

European gas prices surged on Monday as a forecast cold snap in the coming weeks fed fears across the continent’s over depleted supply this winter and costly household bills.

The Dutch month-ahead contract – the European benchmark for gas prices over the next four weeks– rose by as much as 8.6% to €96.08, before settling up 4% at €92.50.

The jump in gas prices comes as much of north-west Europe braces for a tough winter, when energy demand is at its highest.

Europe’s gas supplies have been hit by a slowdown in exports from Qatar due to the war in the Middle East, as well as an increase in consumption during the summer to power refrigeration and cooling during the prolonged heatwave.

Storage levels on the continent are now well below the seasonal average, at about 69% full against a typical level of 80%.

Labour faces double blow over UK fossil fuel projects

Read more

In the UK, energy system operators have said the country will have enough gas and electricity to meet demand during the coldest months, partly because of paying higher market prices than neighbours to secure imports.

However, it means British households will probably pay some of the highest energy bills in Europe this winter.

This week the energy regulator Ofgem is expected to announce a 26% rise in its quarterly price cap from January, adding an extra £443 to an average annual bill for a dual-fuel household.

It could be one of the biggest quarterly price rises on record. The charity Citizens Advice has said it expects a wave of more people seeking emergency help.

The chief executive, Clare Moriarty, said every day its “advisers see people whose budgets have been completely wiped out by years of compounding crises.”

“Millions of households are entering the coldest months of the year with nothing left,” she said.

Last month, the chancellor, John Healey, used his first budget to announce a giveaway of £100 to 20m households in council tax bands A to D to help with energy bills.

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

But Moriarty said that, while the top-up was welcome, it “simply won’t stretch far enough for those who need the most support.”

“Many households will quickly burn through it, leaving them at risk of deeper debt or being unable to top up their prepayment meter just as winter bites.

“The government must take action before the cold weather takes hold. A targeted top-up to the warm home discount and an emergency support credit for prepayment customers are vital, practical lifelines that will stop households being left in the cold and dark this winter.”

Chris O’Shea, the boss of British Gas owner Centrica, has also said he is “hugely concerned” about the forecast jump in energy bills, warning that the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their bills would rise in the new year.

He told the BBC on Sunday that there is a “massive problem” with people not paying their bills in the UK, with some without the means to do so and an “increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills”.

items.title: Trump hosts third crypto gala for meme coin amid conflict of interest outcry
items.summary: Virginia dinner comes as Democrats accuse president of improperly profiting from his cryptocurrency ventures Donald Trump has headlined his third cryptocurrency gala at his ​country club in Virginia, rewarding top holders of his own meme coin, as Democrats accuse the president of improperly profitin…
items.body:
Donald Trump gestures to reporters while taking questions during a news briefing in the White House on Friday in Washington DC. Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Donald Trump gestures to reporters while taking questions during a news briefing in the White House on Friday in Washington DC. Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Trump hosts third crypto gala for meme coin amid conflict of interest outcry

Virginia dinner comes as Democrats accuse president of improperly profiting from his cryptocurrency ventures

Donald Trump is scheduled to headline his third cryptocurrency gala on ⁠Sunday night at his ​country club in Virginia, rewarding top holders of his own meme coin as Democrats accuse the president of improperly profiting from his crypto ventures.

The dinner, set to take place at the Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, will include meet-and-greets with Trump supporters including the boxing champion Floyd Mayweather, Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary, NBA champion Tristan Thompson and mentalist Lior Suchard, according to the event’s website.

The gala’s access and perks are divided by tiers for the 185 holders of $TRUMP, the president’s meme coin. A Trump fragrance, a poster, a “commemorative” ticket, and a “Trump watch” are reserved for 120 attendees. Meanwhile, the top 29 investors are invited to a VIP reception, and the top four will receive a “TRUMP 18K Gold Watch”.

Trump has hosted two similar galas since he took office last year, bringing a flurry of criticism as Democrats accuse Trump and his family of monetizing his brand through an array of equities and crypto ventures while in office.

A statue of Donald Trump holding a bitcoin in recognition of his support for cryptocurrency is displayed on the National Mall in September 2025 in Washington DC. Photograph: Alex Brandon/AP

After sweepingwins in the midterms, Democrats have vowed to investigate conflicts of interest involving Trump and his personal wealth during his presidency. They also say they plan to push for legislation that would ban activities such as the meme coin gala dinner.

“This dinner and scoring mechanism appear carefully constructed to increase investment in $TRUMP, allowing the President to abuse the power of his office to personally enrich himself, as he has throughout this term,” reads a letter sent by Adam Schiff and eight other US senators last month.

Since returning to the White House, Trump has made more than $1bn from his crypto businesses, according to financial disclosures released in June. Trump received more than $500m from his World Liberty Financial business selling new crypto products, and raked another $600m from sales of souvenir-type “meme” coins stamped with Trump’s face. Trump launched his $Trump meme coin days before his inauguration.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Interest in the $TRUMP coin dinner has plummeted, with contestants’ combined holdings dropping from $148m in May 2025 to $8.6m in this month’s gala.

More than half of the digital wallets publicly listed on the contest leaderboard for Sunday’s dinner are tied directly to crypto exchanges that bar US-based users, indicating they ‌are linked to foreign nationals, according to an analysis of blockchain data prepared for Reuters by the nonpartisan, non-profit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.

Demonstrators hold up mock cryptocurrency during a rally Against Trump's crypto dealings at the Trump National Golf Club in May 2025 in Virginia. Photograph: Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Public Citizen

“Neither the President nor his family ⁠has ever engaged — or will ever engage — in conflicts of interest,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Reuters ​earlier this year. “President Trump proudly made ​the United States the crypto capital of the world ​through executive actions.“

The Trump family’s other crypto-connected equities and ventures have also fallen in value to record ​lows. Together, outside investors in their ‌five main crypto and ​crypto-linked projects have lost more than $5bn​, according to a Reuters analysis.

The Trump meme coin has earned the Trump family at least $635m, according to the president’s June financial disclosure statement. In total, the Trumps had earned at least $2.3bn through April from their four main crypto ventures, including the meme coin.

The president’s stake in a fifth crypto-linked venture, Trump Media & Technology Group, is worth about $430m.

Reuters contributed reporting

items.title: Up to 1.1m people eligible to join class action against Jetstar over alleged failure to refund Covid flights
items.summary: Jetstar accused of issuing customers credits instead of cash refunds for flights cancelled between 2020 and late 2022 Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast More than 1 million Jetstar customers could be eligible to join a class action alleging the airline failed to refund them…
items.body:
Echo Law is leading a class action against Jetstar over allegations it failed to refund customers for cancelled flights during the pandemic. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

Echo Law is leading a class action against Jetstar over allegations it failed to refund customers for cancelled flights during the pandemic. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

Up to 1.1m people eligible to join class action against Jetstar over alleged failure to refund Covid flights

Jetstar accused of issuing customers credits instead of cash refunds for flights cancelled between 2020 and late 2022

• Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

More than 1 million Jetstar customers could be eligible to join a class action alleging the airline failed to refund them for flights it cancelled during the pandemic, the firm leading the lawsuit has said.

The federal court on Monday confirmed it had ordered notices be sent to customers informing them of their eligibility to participate in, or opt out of, the lawsuit, with a potential trial set for March 2027.

Echo Law, the firm leading the class action, said it wanted to alert the public to the notices – which were due to be distributed by 4 December – to ensure they understood it was not a scam. About 1.1 million people will receive them.

The class action alleges Jetstar issued customers flight credits instead of the cash refunds they were entitled to for flights cancelled between 2020 and late 2022, after cancelling thousands of scheduled domestic and international flights.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email

Echo Law ran a separate class action against Qantas over its handling of Covid-19 travel credits, which the airline in March agreed to settle for $105m with no admission of liability.

In its case against Jetstar, the firm alleges the airline breached its legal obligations to customers by failing to provide refunds for cancelled flights, instead offering customers credit vouchers.

It alleges Jetstar misled customers and engaged in unconscionable conduct in breach of Australian consumer law.

It also alleges that, by holding customers’ funds that ought to have been refunded, Jetstar unlawfully benefited from this conduct.

Jetstar has denied the allegations and is defending the class action

“During the Covid-19 pandemic, Jetstar took a range of steps to respond to rapidly changing travel restrictions, while continuing to support customers affected by disruptions,” a spokesperson for the airline said.

“We provided customers with a range of options during this period depending on the circumstances, including travel credits, fee-free flight changes and refunds.

They said customers with a Jetstar Covid-19 voucher could use it whenever they were ready to, as the airline had removed the expiry date in 2023.

However, Andrew Paull, a partner at Echo Law, alleged Jetstar’s policy of “pushing” customers to accept vouchers was designed to preserve the airline’s cash position.

“It held onto ordinary Australian’s [sic] money and expected customers to just be happy with credits, or in some cases nothing, when we allege they were entitled to cash refunds,” he alleged.

Paull alleged many customers had ended up paying Jetstar more than their original booking to use their credits on new fares, as they were led to believe they had little choice but to do so in order to avoid losing the value of their flights.

The firm’s lawsuit against Jetstar is scheduled for mediation in December and is expected to go to trial if the parties fail to reach an agreement.

Echo Law said the litigation funder Court House Capital was backing its class action against Jetstar.

Court House Capital’s chief investment officer, Heather Collins, accused Jetstar of seeking to “delay resolution while continuing to hold onto money that belongs to Australian families”.

items.body:
Many Queensland football club members say the state governing body, Football Queensland, charges unreasonably high fees and is unaccountable. Photograph: Natee127/Getty Images

Many Queensland football club members say the state governing body, Football Queensland, charges unreasonably high fees and is unaccountable. Photograph: Natee127/Getty Images

Clubs and families revolt as Football Queensland charges $5 a head to watch children play

Gate fee comes on top of annual cost of between $300 and $700 per family

• Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Football clubs representing hundreds of thousands of players are preparing to break away from Football Queensland this week, saying the state governing body charges unreasonably high fees and is unaccountable.

Some parents and siblings are charged a $5 gate fee to watch children’s matches in parts of regional Queensland.

The gate fee comes on top of an annual cost of between $300 and $700 per family, depending on player age, club and other factors, and a range of other fees, fines and charges. Many football club members say they see little in return for the thousands they pay in fees.

Jessy Mulla is president of Leichhardt Football Club Cairns Incorporated, which was recently disaffiliated from the statewide body.

Football Queensland, which manages the club, introduced a gate fee in 2024 in order to pay for improvements to the ground, Endeavour Park, in Manunda, such as cleaning toilets, employing a full-time gardener, and “increased shade structures and grandstands”, at a quoted price of $20,000 each.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email

With a few hundred people attending most weekends, the amount raised through gate fees must be substantial, Mulla said.

But there had been “very, very” little improvement to the ground since, Mulla said.

“That’s why everyone asks where’s the money being spent? Where’s the money that gets raised? Where is it going?”

Under Football Queensland’s policy, registered coaches and team managers, referees, volunteers and children under 15 enter free. Pensioners get a discount, paying $4.

The sport’s governing body in the state is a member of the national football body, Football Australia. It provides a range of services for typically volunteer-run clubs, including managing competitions, governance, and developing player professional pathways, as well as managing some facilities.

Clubs have to pay an annual fee to affiliate with the central body, which they pass on to players.

A spokesperson for Football Queensland said the body was “continuing to progress the delivery and investment of long-term infrastructure projects and facility enhancements” in line with its regional facility master plan.

The spokesperson said three levels of government had invested $7.9m into regional Football Queensland facilities since 2023. The central body had also contributed $4.9m in operational costs and capital investment in regional Queensland during the same period, they said.

“A $5 gate fee (or $80 season pass) is consistent with other sporting codes and contributes to FQ’s master plan delivery, helping to offset grounds maintenance and operational expenses,” they said.

It recently created controversy by proposing to charge a $35 per player fee for summer competitions organised by the clubs themselves, and proposing other fee increases, which have since been dropped.

A rebel faction of football clubs is preparing to break away from Football Queensland this week, complaining of a lack of input and transparency of the central body.

Bardon Latrobe football club president, Gerard Doyle, said more than 100 clubs – a majority – had joined a movement pushing for reform.

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

Doyle estimated that the breakaway clubs represented more than 100,000 football players.

The group is now negotiating with the central body via a law firm. Others were on the fence, he said.

According to its bylaws, Football Queensland’s governing committee must hold elections for new board members this month.

But the board has yet to call elections.

Doyle said that it was now impossible for the board to meet its bylaws, given the need for a one-week period for people to nominate.

Meanwhile, clubs have been given until Wednesday, 25 November, to re-affiliate with the central authority, after an extension to the sign-up period.

Clubs have two options, he said.

“Number one is Football Australia comes in today or tomorrow, two days, and says we will facilitate open and free elections,” he said.

If that doesn’t happen, the clubs will refuse to affiliate and pay their fees and instead create their own rival central body, he said.

“I sound like I’m in a dictatorship in an African nation here, fighting for basic rights.

“To me, it just feels, I’m going to say un-Australian … it’s undemocratic.”

items.body: In today’s newsletter: The prime minister has reopened the debate over a future relationship with a changed EU – as the bloc faces the rise of the far right, a protectionist economic agenda and growing defence ambitions Good morning. Nobody really wants to think about Brexit any more, save for the original Brexiters, who seem delighted that Andy Burnham’s “reset” with the EU has given them an excuse to get the old gang back together. But arguments about whether the UK should rejoin the EU will reignite in parliament this week, as Burnham briefs MPs on the deal he agreed on Friday. That deal wasn’t so much a victory as the culmination of Keir Starmer’s incrementalist approach to UK-EU relations. Its core agreements haven’t been ratified by member states yet, and the EU won’t sign them off until Britain resolves a dispute over tuition fees for European students. Burnham is apparently “determined” to take the UK back into the EU, but don’t expect any progress on that before the next general election. The proposed deal failed to endorse a away from fossil fuels that more than 130 countries demanded.
